directions.hypothesis: The within-study predictive power of local environment and geography for eukaryotic fraction is mostly carried by sampling campaign; with campaign held out, predictive power falls to near zero, as it does across studies.
directions.outcomes: Support: held-out-campaign predictive power drops to about zero or below while campaign-labelled models keep the earlier within-study gain. Refute: environment and geography keep their predictive power when campaigns are held out.
directions.prior_work: 41854267 estimates prokaryotic fractions by biome across metagenomes but does not test whether campaign explains within-study environmental signal.
directions.question: Within the NEON soil study, does local environment and geography still predict the eukaryotic read fraction once sampling campaign or batch is accounted for?
directions.readiness_basis: Biosample and run tables appear in the catalog, but the GOTTCHA2 output table was not shown and models must be fitted.
directions.test: Take the eukaryotic fraction per run from the GOTTCHA2 taxonomy output, the only classifier reported to give a usable fraction, treated as relative rather than absolute. Join to NMDC biosample, study and data-generation tables for NEON soil runs, with Kraken and Centrifuge outputs used only as predictors if suitable. Compare models using environment and geography alone against models holding out whole collection dates or campaigns. The catalog did not show the GOTTCHA2 table, so its location must be confirmed.
directions.title: Does sampling campaign, not local environment, explain eukaryotic read fraction within a single soil study?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, apparent environmental drivers of eukaryotic contamination in prokaryote-targeted metagenomes are batch effects, and metagenome users should model campaign before interpreting environment.

directions.hypothesis: Most plant-association markers separate genera, not species within genera, so a model that controls for ancestry and corrects for the many markers tested retains few markers.
directions.outcomes: Support: few markers remain after ancestry control and correction. Refute: many markers still separate plant from non-plant species within genera.
directions.prior_work: 29255260 and 22792073 describe plant-associated genomic features but do not test whether signals persist within genera.
directions.question: Once shared ancestry is controlled, do plant-associated species differ from non-plant relatives in the same genus in plant-association marker genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Taxonomy and tree-distance tables are in the catalog; marker tables were not shown and the models need running.
directions.test: Using GTDB species clades and metadata in the pangenome collection, rerun the within-genus comparison with many more shuffles than the earlier 200, a regression that uses genome tree distances to control ancestry, and a correction for the 15 markers tested together.
directions.title: Is plant association a genus-level trait, with species inside a genus not distinguished by marker genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that plant adaptation signals in genomes largely reflect which lineages occupy plants, changing how marker panels are used to predict plant lifestyle.

directions.hypothesis: Species clades with more open pangenomes carry more latent pathways even after controlling for phylogenetic relatedness and for how many strains were fitness-tested.
directions.outcomes: Support: the positive association survives controls. Refute: it vanishes with ancestry or testing depth.
directions.prior_work: 24910088 explains biosynthetic gene loss but does not relate latent pathway fraction to pangenome openness.
directions.question: Is the higher fraction of fitness-neutral complete pathways in species with open pangenomes independent of shared ancestry?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway, pangenome and experiment tables are in the catalog; the controlled model has to be built.
directions.test: For the 48 Fitness Browser organisms, classify GapMind pathways as latent or active using fitness data, add pangenome openness per species clade, and refit with ancestry control and tested-strain count as covariates.
directions.title: Does pangenome openness predict how many complete metabolic pathways are dispensable?
directions.why_it_matters: It would link gene-flow-rich lifestyles to metabolic redundancy, suggesting that open pangenomes allow pathway stockpiling rather than reflecting lab artifacts.

directions.hypothesis: Removing clinical and human-associated genomes raises the environment effect on gene content above the very small median seen across species.
directions.outcomes: Support: the environment effect and share of species with detectable effects rise after exclusion. Refute: results stay near zero.
directions.prior_work: 37189129 finds geography rather than lifestyle structures symbiont populations, but not with embedding-based environment effects.
directions.question: Does excluding clinical and human-associated genomes strengthen the relationship between environmental embeddings and gene content?
directions.readiness_basis: Embedding, environment and tree tables are in the catalog; coverage of genomes is partial.
directions.test: In species with satellite embeddings, compare environment versus phylogeny effects on gene content for all genomes and for non-clinical genomes, using habitat classes from NCBI environment attributes and tree distances.
directions.title: Does clinical sampling bias hide environmental signal in gene content?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, weak environment effects reflect a biased genome sample, and environment-based inference should be restricted to environmental isolates.

directions.hypothesis: Modules from independent component analysis (ICA) that are mostly accessory genes show stronger co-inheritance than matched random gene sets and than co-fit pairs, even after accounting for how common each gene is across genomes.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory modules beat prevalence-matched random sets and beat pairs in most organisms. Refute: the advantage disappears once prevalence is matched, which would mean the signal is a prevalence artefact.
directions.prior_work: Earlier pangenome co-occurrence work (34499026, 32100706, 40304385) tests gene pairs; this tests whether co-regulated modules with a prevalence control are the unit of co-inheritance.
directions.question: Are co-regulated multi-gene modules inherited together across strains more strongly than co-fit gene pairs, and is the effect concentrated in accessory modules?
directions.readiness_basis: Source tables are in the catalog, but per-organism presence-matrix extraction on Spark was slow and limited the earlier sample.
directions.test: For the Fitness Browser organisms with module and co-fitness data (for example Btheta and Korea), map genes to pangenome clusters. Compute co-inheritance for modules, co-fit pairs and prevalence-matched random sets. Stratify by core fraction, and restrict to accessory modules and species with enough accessory variation.
directions.title: Do multi-gene regulatory modules, rather than co-fit pairs, mark the units that selection keeps together across genomes?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, the selective units behind gene-content evolution are modules, not pairs, and lab fitness data could be used to predict which genes travel together in pangenomes.

directions.hypothesis: After conditioning on core-genome phylogenetic distance, adaptive COG categories (defense, unknown function, mobile elements) still differ between ecotypes by more than housekeeping categories do, though the gap shrinks.
directions.outcomes: Support: adaptive categories keep a larger difference after control. Refute: the difference falls to the housekeeping level, which would point to demographic structure.
directions.prior_work: Single-taxon ecotype studies (31611653, 31615877) show non-random gene content; this tests a multi-species adaptive-versus-housekeeping contrast with phylogenetic control.
directions.question: Do adaptive functional categories still differentiate gene-content ecotypes more than housekeeping categories once population structure from the core genome is accounted for?
directions.readiness_basis: Tree distances and annotations are in the catalog, but the earlier sample was limited by Spark cluster load.
directions.test: For the 12 analysed species, use pairwise tree distances between genomes. Permute ecotype labels within phylogenetic clusters and recompute the size of each category's difference between ecotypes. Compare adaptive versus housekeeping categories with and without control. Add habitat metadata from the environment tables where present.
directions.title: Does gene-content ecotype differentiation survive control for within-species phylogeny in adaptive categories?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate ecological adaptation from demographic substructure and show whether annotation gaps hide niche genes.

directions.hypothesis: Disabling automatic broadcasting prevents failures when a very large table would be broadcast, but causes hangs on mid-size joins where broadcasting is cheap.
directions.outcomes: Support: the setting wins on the largest join and loses on mid-size ones. Refute: results are the same by size, so the earlier discrepancy came from session state.
directions.question: Why do projects disagree on whether turning off automatic broadcasting prevents failures or causes notebook hangs?
directions.readiness_basis: Controlled benchmark runs are needed; the catalog shows only reported runtimes with no baseline.
directions.test: Run one fixed UniProt-style join and several mid-size joins in clean sessions with the setting at -1 and at default, plus explicit hints. Record query plans, failures and hang time. Also run the presence-matrix extraction for one organism with and without hints.
directions.title: Does disabling automatic broadcast joins help or hang Spark joins, depending on table size?
directions.why_it_matters: It would replace conflicting advice with a rule keyed to table size, saving analysts lost notebook time.

directions.hypothesis: If the GC shift is carried mainly by core genes shared by all strains, it points to sequence-level processes rather than gene gain and loss. If it vanishes once accessory genes are removed, it is a by-product of gene-content differences.
directions.outcomes: Support: the association persists in core-gene GC in most species and is weak in accessory GC. Refute: the association is confined to accessory-gene GC or disappears in both partitions. Either result is informative. Neither establishes the cause of a core-gene shift.
directions.prior_work: PMID 33166245 links plasmid GC to niche across Lactobacillaceae species, and PMID 34100697 links GC to lifestyle; neither splits within-species GC into core and accessory parts.
directions.question: Within bacterial species where GC content varies with isolation source, is the shift carried by core-genome sequence, by the accessory genes that are gained or lost, or by both?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene cluster core/accessory flags and sequences are in the catalog, but per-genome partitioned GC would have to be computed; the catalog did not show a precomputed partition.
directions.test: For the species with an isolation-source GC association after ANI-cluster control, compute per-genome GC separately for core gene clusters and for accessory gene clusters. Repeat the isolation-source association, with the same phylogenetic control, on each partition. Compare the share of species with an association in each partition. Also use the within-species tree distances to check that the result holds when phylogeny is modelled continuously.
directions.title: Does within-species GC variation with isolation source arise in core genes or in gene gain and loss?
directions.why_it_matters: GC appeared more environment-responsive within species than gene presence/absence, which sits in tension with phylogeny dominating gene content. Locating the GC signal would show which kind of variation tracks environment. Whether this reflects adaptation, mutation or recombination bias is a possible interpretation to test afterward, not something this analysis settles.

directions.hypothesis: Accessory genes are shared among same-environment strains only about as much as chance predicts after accounting for phylogeny, in both open and closed pangenomes, consistent with opportunistic transfer.
directions.outcomes: Support: same-environment sharing is near the permutation null in species at all openness levels. Refute: a subset of species, or of gene categories, shows clear same-environment sharing that is independent of phylogeny. Refuting would imply that the null cross-species result hid directed transfer in some genes.
directions.prior_work: PMID 23332119 shows habitat structuring of gene transfer and PMID 25311532 found no niche-specific genomic features in one species; this direction tests directed versus opportunistic exchange across species of differing openness.
directions.question: If horizontal gene transfer were ecologically directed, accessory genes should be shared more among strains from the same environment. Is that so in species that differ in openness?
directions.readiness_basis: Pangenome summary tables, gene clusters and tree distances are in the catalog, but the gene-by-genome matrices and the permutation tests would need to be built.
directions.test: Choose species with ecotype results spanning low to high openness. Within each, test whether pairwise accessory-gene-content similarity rises with shared isolation environment beyond what tree distance predicts. Use a permutation that shuffles environment labels within ANI clusters. Then ask whether the genes driving any signal are enriched in particular functional categories (COG, Pfam). Compare the size of the signal with openness.
directions.title: Is pangenome openness unrelated to environment because gene exchange is opportunistic rather than directed?
directions.why_it_matters: Openness did not track either the environment effect or the phylogeny effect across species. That is compatible with opportunistic transfer, but the species-level summary may hide gene-level structure. A gene-level test would separate the two explanations.

directions.hypothesis: After regressing out within-species tree distance, ecotype membership still predicts isolation environment in at least some of the ten species with distinct metabolic clusters.
directions.outcomes: Support: environment association stays beyond the permutation null in several species and the culture experiment shows growth differences matching the pathway gap. Refute: the association disappears once clades are controlled, or the predicted growth differences are absent.
directions.prior_work: PMID 35575545 shows ecotypes evolving under fluctuating resources in experiments; this direction asks whether natural pathway clusters track environment beyond lineage.
directions.question: Are the pathway-based ecotypes seen in Salmonella and Phenylobacterium associated with environment once within-species phylogeny is modelled, or do they only mirror lineage?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway completeness and tree distances are in the catalog; the corrected association tests need to be run, and the culture step needs new measurements.
directions.test: For the ten species with metabolic clusters, build GapMind pathway-completeness profiles per genome. Test whether cluster membership is associated with isolation environment, with tree distance from the phylogenetic trees as covariate or via permutation within tree clades. Compare with a null from clusters made on random pathway subsets. Follow with a culture experiment on contrasting strains in Salmonella, grown on carbon sources whose pathways differ between clusters.
directions.title: Do within-species metabolic ecotypes survive correction for phylogenetic structure?
directions.why_it_matters: All ten target species showed metabolic clustering, but phylogeny dominates gene content in 60.5% of species. Whether the clusters are ecological or lineage substructure decides if they count as evidence of adaptation.

directions.hypothesis: Truly dark genes lie closer to mobile-element genes than length-matched annotated genes do, and this holds after controlling for GC deviation, which can also reflect membrane-protein composition.
directions.outcomes: Support: dark genes are closer to mobile elements and more often accessory than matched controls, across several organisms. Refute: the proximity vanishes after length and composition matching, or comes only from Methanococcus, pointing to annotation lag or database bias.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 37821698 describe dark genes and unannotated families, but neither tests mobile-element proximity against matched annotated genes.
directions.question: Are genes with no annotation and no fitness phenotype physically clustered in islands near mobile elements, as recent acquisition predicts, or is their accessory enrichment explained by gene length or composition?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene coordinates, pangenome class and Bakta calls appear in the catalog tables; ortholog links for uncovered organisms were not shown.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser gene table, take truly dark genes and annotation-lag genes, using gene coordinates per organism. Compute distance to the nearest mobile-element-annotated gene and compare with length-matched annotated genes. Link to the pangenome gene clusters for core/accessory class and Bakta product calls. Stratify by organism so Methanococcus, which holds over half the dark genes, does not dominate.
directions.title: Do truly dark genes sit in genomic islands near mobile elements, indicating recent acquisition?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, dark matter is partly a signature of recent horizontal acquisition, and annotation effort should focus on mobile-linked islands rather than assuming annotation lag.

directions.hypothesis: The depletion persists after excluding genes in operons with annotated neighbours (polar-effect candidates) and after matching for number of conditions tested per organism, and dark genes instead show strong phenotypes in carbon or nitrogen conditions.
directions.outcomes: Support: depletion holds in polar-filtered, condition-matched data. Refute: it disappears once polar candidates or condition depth are controlled, meaning the earlier result was an artifact.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 22125499 report phenotypes for poorly annotated genes but do not compare dark and annotation-lag genes by condition class.
directions.question: Does the depletion of strong-phenotype truly dark genes in stress conditions reflect real biology, such as niche-specific roles, or limited condition coverage and polar effects?
directions.readiness_basis: Experiment and gene tables are in the catalog; fitness value tables and operon calls were not shown and may need computing.
directions.test: Using Fitness Browser experiments and fitness data, classify conditions by class, flag dark genes adjacent to annotated same-strand genes as possible polar cases, and compare strong-phenotype rates by condition class between truly dark and annotation-lag genes within each organism. Then pick dark genes with phenotypes in unusual conditions and test them with targeted mutants in a tractable organism.
directions.title: Why are truly dark genes with strong phenotypes depleted in stress conditions?
directions.why_it_matters: It would redirect screens for dark-gene function away from standard stress panels and toward nutrient and niche-specific conditions.

directions.hypothesis: Core genes with shallow alignment depth are concentrated in a few under-sampled lineages, and their predicted structures match known folds more often than their sequence annotation does.
directions.outcomes: Support: enrichment in a few lineages and frequent fold matches. Refute: even spread across lineages and no fold matches, implying novel folds or poor predictions.
directions.prior_work: The AlphaFold papers 34599769, 34791371 and 41273079 describe prediction and databases, not alignment depth by pangenome class or lineage.
directions.question: Where do conserved core genes with very shallow alignment depth and mostly hypothetical annotation concentrate taxonomically, and does structure prediction give them function clues?
directions.readiness_basis: Tables are in the catalog, but Foldseek runs and the cluster-to-UniProt mapping require compute.
directions.test: Join the AlphaFold alignment-depth table to pangenome gene clusters via UniProt links, select core clusters with shallow alignment depth and hypothetical Bakta calls, and map them onto GTDB taxonomy to test lineage enrichment against all core clusters. For a sample, run Foldseek against structure databases and check domain hits in InterProScan.
directions.title: Do structurally novel proteins with shallow alignments concentrate in specific lineages?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate a sequence-database gap in particular lineages from truly new protein folds, and show where annotation effort pays off.

directions.hypothesis: On a shared gene set and test count, Pfam recovers the lipoprotein and toluene-tolerance terms that old KEGG found, and adds more specific terms than InterProScan GO.
directions.outcomes: Support: Pfam recovers KEGG terms plus new specific ones with a low permuted rate. Refute: Pfam misses them or inflates hits in random sets.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 supplies fitness data for unknown genes but does not compare annotation sources for enrichment.
directions.question: Do differences between annotation sources in cofitness enrichment reflect resolution or just coverage?
directions.readiness_basis: Domain tables are in the catalog; the cofitness networks and enrichment need computing.
directions.test: For antimicrobial resistance cofitness neighbourhoods in Fitness Browser organisms, run enrichment with Pfam domains, old KEGG and InterProScan GO using the same genes, background and threshold. Compare terms recovered and test against permuted random gene sets to measure Pfam overcounting.
directions.title: Does Pfam give more mechanism-specific enrichment than legacy KEGG in cofitness networks?
directions.why_it_matters: It would guide which annotation source to use for function inference from fitness data.

directions.hypothesis: Genes that deletion calls essential but transposon screening calls dispensable carry insertions concentrated at gene ends or between domains, so truncated proteins keep enough function to grow.
directions.outcomes: Support: insertions in the first group sit near the 3' end or in linker regions, and partial alleles grow. Refute: insertions are spread evenly and partial alleles fail, which would point to condition or noise differences instead.
directions.prior_work: 18319726 built the ADP1 deletion collection and 25374488 profiled it with multiomics; neither tests whether insertion position explains disagreement with transposon calls.
directions.question: Why do transposon screening and complete gene deletion call different genes essential in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, and does tolerance of partly working proteins explain the gap?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog did not show ADP1 insertion positions or deletion calls as tables, and partial alleles would need to be built; Fitness Browser tables support only the cross-organism comparison.
directions.test: Take the ADP1 genes where deletion says essential but transposon screening says dispensable (211 genes) and the reverse set (293 genes). Map insertion positions inside each gene. As a cross-organism comparison, use Fitness Browser gene coordinates and fitness values to see whether essential-like genes with weak fitness effects are short or have insertions only near gene ends. Then build partial alleles for a panel of the first group and test growth on the knockout-collection medium.
directions.title: Do transposon insertions that leave partial protein function explain disagreement with clean deletions in ADP1?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, transposon essentiality calls would be known to undercall genes with separable domains, and fitness from such screens should not be read as lethality without insertion-position checks.

directions.hypothesis: Mobile-element genes show cost in many unrelated experiments within the same organism, whereas costly conserved genes show cost only in a few condition types.
directions.outcomes: Support: mobile-element genes are costly across many experiments and condition types. Refute: their cost comes mostly from one experiment or one condition class, as for the conserved group.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 supplies the fitness data and 22448042 proposes adaptive gene loss; neither asks how widely mobile-element genes are costly across conditions.
directions.question: Costly but dispensable genes are mostly mobile-element debris, so does their cost appear everywhere or only under particular conditions?
directions.readiness_basis: Gene-level fitness, experiment descriptions, gene descriptions and orthologs are in the catalog tables listed.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, take genes with positive fitness in any experiment. Split them into mobile-element keyword genes and conserved genes using gene descriptions and ortholog tables. For each gene, count independent experiments and distinct condition types with positive fitness, and compare the two groups within each organism.
directions.title: Is the fitness cost of mobile-element genes concentrated in particular growth conditions?
directions.why_it_matters: A broad cost would support steady genome-expansion pressure from horizontal transfer. A condition-limited cost would suggest that the cost label partly reflects noise in single experiments or specific stresses.

directions.hypothesis: Fitness magnitude predicts core status better than condition type in most organisms, so the DvH result is general and not a feature of one small pangenome.
directions.outcomes: Support: magnitude beats condition class in most organisms. Refute: condition class adds clear predictive value in several organisms, which would indicate niche-specific selection.
directions.prior_work: 37065130 gives DvH fitness data and 29769716 gives multi-organism fitness data; neither compares magnitude with condition type for predicting conservation.
directions.question: Across bacteria with fitness data, is a gene's pangenome conservation better predicted by how large its fitness effect is or by what kind of condition revealed it?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and pangenome tables are in the catalog, but linking Fitness Browser genes to pangenome clusters needs a mapping step not shown in the catalog.
directions.test: For Fitness Browser organisms linked to pangenome clades, compute each gene's strongest fitness effect and its condition class (stress, nutrient, carbon source) from the experiment table. Fit models of core versus accessory status with magnitude alone, condition class alone, and both. Compare them within each organism, especially those with many genomes, and include the DvH field-stress genes.
directions.title: Does the size of a gene's fitness effect predict conservation better than the condition tested?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that the core genome reflects general functional importance rather than niche-specific selection, and that environment-matched assays add little for predicting conservation.

directions.hypothesis: Efflux genes are the only mechanism class whose fitness effect changes sign between antibiotic and non-antibiotic conditions across organisms, while baseline cost stays similar across classes.
directions.outcomes: Support: only efflux shows a clear flip within organisms, with equal baseline cost across classes. Refute: the flip disappears within organisms or appears in enzymatic genes once antibiotic class is matched.
directions.prior_work: 25861385 and 20208551 cover resistance cost in general, and 26203082 covers in vivo fitness; none compares conditional fitness flips across mechanism classes.
directions.question: Resistance mechanism does not explain baseline fitness cost of AMR genes, but efflux genes flip more strongly under antibiotics, so is mechanism a condition-dependent trait?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and AMR annotation tables are in the catalog, but gene-to-cluster mapping and mechanism classification must be built.
directions.test: Annotate AMR genes in Fitness Browser organisms with pangenome AMR calls. Split experiments into antibiotic and non-antibiotic. Compare fitness shifts by mechanism class within organisms that have many AMR genes, and test whether efflux pumps of broad and narrow spectrum differ.
directions.title: Does resistance mechanism matter for fitness only when antibiotics are present?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate baseline cost from conditional benefit and show that mechanism predicts conservation through conditional benefit, not constant cost.

directions.hypothesis: Essential genes lacking a pangenome match or labeled auxiliary mostly share domains or pathway roles with essential core genes, so grouping them by function removes much of the apparent strain specificity.
directions.outcomes: Support: a large share of these genes fall into core essential functional groups beyond matched random genes. Refute: they remain unassigned or fall into mobile or unrelated functions at the matched-gene rate.
directions.prior_work: 36097170 shows essentiality depends on the pan-genome in one species; this direction tests whether functional grouping explains strain-specific essentials across many organisms.
directions.question: Essential genes outside the core genome are explained only partly, so are they strain-specific versions of core functions?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotation tables are in the catalog, but essential gene calls and pangenome links must be derived from fitness data.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser organisms, list essential genes with no pangenome cluster match or auxiliary status. Assign them to functional groups using SEED roles and KEGG groups, and compare against essential core genes in the same organism. Test whether the share assigned to a core essential function exceeds that of random non-essential genes of matched length.
directions.title: Are strain-specific essential genes variants of core machinery rather than unique functions?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that essentiality is conserved at the function level even when genes differ, and would give a route to annotate the poorly characterized essential-unmapped genes.

directions.hypothesis: Costly+dispensable genes that are not mobile-element-annotated sit near annotated mobile elements or have atypical GC far more often than costly+conserved genes. Their burden should also stay when the one-experiment cost rule is replaced by a rule requiring replication across several experiments.
directions.outcomes: Support: the enrichment holds under the replicated cost rule and extends to unannotated genes by neighbourhood. Refute: the enrichment vanishes under the replicated rule, or unannotated costly genes are not near mobile elements, suggesting noise or metabolic decay.
directions.prior_work: Black Queen work (22448042) and pangenome essentiality (36097170) address gene loss, but neither tests whether costly dispensable genes are mobile-element debris; this direction tests that with a replicated cost definition.
directions.question: Do costly but non-conserved genes in Fitness Browser bacteria persist because they are selfish mobile elements that have not yet been purged, rather than degrading metabolic pathways?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and pangenome tables appear in the catalog, but linking genes to pangenome clusters and computing neighbourhoods requires new compute.
directions.test: For Fitness Browser organisms, classify genes as costly if they show a fitness gain in at least 2 independent experiments, then as conserved or dispensable using pangenome core status. Compare keyword-based and neighbourhood-based mobile-element signals (distance to transposase, integrase and phage genes; GC deviation) using the Fitness Browser gene and SEED annotations and the pangenome gene cluster core flags. Repeat with the original single-experiment rule.
directions.title: Are costly yet dispensable genes mainly selfish mobile elements still awaiting loss?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that horizontal gene transfer expansion, not adaptive loss of metabolic functions, is the main source of costly accessory genes. That would redirect how gene loss theories are applied to pangenomes.

directions.hypothesis: Within the subset of modules that have many accessory genes, family breadth still does not predict core fraction, so conservation is a gene property; modules with accessory members will instead show stronger co-inheritance than core modules.
directions.outcomes: Support: no breadth-core gradient in the restricted set, and co-inheritance tracks accessory fraction. Refute: a clear positive gradient emerges once the ceiling is removed.
directions.prior_work: Pangenome co-occurrence papers (34499026, 32100706) and module detection work (29545622) do not test breadth against core fraction; this direction removes the ceiling effect.
directions.question: Is the lack of relationship between module family breadth and core fraction a ceiling effect of a high core baseline, or does it show that conservation belongs to individual genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Module assignments and pangenome flags exist per the findings, but the catalog did not show module tables, so they may need to be regenerated.
directions.test: Using Fitness Browser ICA module families and ortholog tables, restrict to modules with a substantial accessory share. Test breadth against core fraction using pangenome core flags, and compare against a null that preserves each organism's core baseline. Then relate module co-inheritance across genomes to accessory fraction.
directions.title: Why do cofitness modules show no link between cross-organism breadth and conservation?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, shared regulation across organisms does not constrain gene retention, and module conservation cannot be used to infer which gene sets are selected together. If a gradient appears, module scope matters.

directions.hypothesis: Flagellar genes join AMR support networks because both are neutral under most lab conditions. A fitness-variance-matched set of other dispensable gene classes will show the same enrichment, and it will vanish when only antibiotic experiments are used.
directions.outcomes: Support: enrichment disappears after matching and is absent in antibiotic-only subsets. Refute: flagellar enrichment persists above the matched null, pointing to a real link between resistance and motility.
directions.prior_work: 31501286 links resistance regulators to flagellar repression in Salmonella, and 28542589 validates regulatory predictions with fitness data; neither tests whether network-level enrichment is a dispensability artefact.
directions.question: Is the enrichment of flagellar motility terms in antimicrobial resistance cofitness networks caused by flagellar genes being dispensable in lab conditions?
directions.readiness_basis: Cofitness, experiment and gene tables are in the catalog for Fitness Browser organisms.
directions.test: For organisms where flagellar terms were enriched, rebuild AMR cofitness partner sets with partners matched on mean fitness and variance. Compute flagellar enrichment separately in antibiotic experiments and in other experiments, and compare with enrichment for other dispensable classes such as histidine and tryptophan biosynthesis.
directions.title: Do AMR support networks reflect flagellar dispensability rather than shared regulation?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate true functional coupling of resistance and motility, as seen for MarA/SoxS repression of flagella in Salmonella, from a data artefact. It would show how far cofitness networks can be read as regulatory networks.

directions.hypothesis: Metal-specific genes are more often accessory and mobile-element-linked than general sick genes, and essential-metal genes carry the larger core shift, because they serve ancient metal homeostasis rather than detoxification.
directions.outcomes: Support: metal-specific genes are more accessory and mobile-linked, and essential-metal genes keep the core shift in 3 or more organisms. Refute: no mobile-element difference, or the essential-toxic contrast depends on one organism.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 12829273 describe fitness data and efflux systems but not core versus accessory status of metal-specific genes.
directions.question: Do metal-specific fitness genes differ from general sick genes in core status because they are accessory efflux and uptake systems acquired by horizontal transfer?
directions.readiness_basis: Metal-condition fitness and pangenome tables are in the catalog, but gene-class labelling and neighbourhood analysis need compute.
directions.test: Across Fitness Browser organisms with metal experiments, label genes as metal-specific, shared-stress or general sick. Compare core fraction, nearness to mobile-element genes, and annotation keywords using pangenome core flags and SEED annotations. Fit metal class (essential vs toxic) with organism as a random effect, excluding single-organism metals.
directions.title: Why do metal-specific genes lean less toward the core genome than general stress genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether metal tolerance is a conserved core capability or a patchy acquired trait, and why bioleaching specialists show no extra signal.

directions.hypothesis: Complex I fitness defects scale with the NADH generated per carbon source, so acetate and succinate defects equal or exceed those on aromatics, and the DUF proteins ACIAD3137 and ACIAD2176 share this pattern.
directions.outcomes: Support: defect size tracks NADH yield, and DUF homologs cofit with nuo elsewhere. Refute: aromatics remain worse after controlling for yield, or DUF homologs show no cofitness.
directions.prior_work: 18319726 and 25374488 phenotype ADP1 on quinate but do not report Complex I fitness or flux-load dependence.
directions.question: Is Complex I needed on aromatics because of the NADH flux they produce, with the defect tracking NADH yield across carbon sources?
directions.readiness_basis: The cross-organism analysis uses catalog tables, but the NADH and mutant growth measurements are not in the catalog.
directions.test: Using Fitness Browser nuo orthologs and cofitness across organisms, regress Complex I fitness on estimated NADH yield per carbon source, controlling for organism. Check whether homologs of ACIAD3137 and ACIAD2176 cofit with nuo genes in other organisms. Then measure NADH/NAD+ ratio and nuo or NDH-2 mutant growth on quinate, acetate and glucose in ADP1.
directions.title: Does the Complex I fitness defect reflect NADH flux load rather than aromatic substrate?
directions.why_it_matters: It would replace an aromatic-specific explanation with a general redox-load one, and flag candidate accessory factors of Complex I.

directions.hypothesis: Costly-but-conserved genes show fitness defects under field-relevant or ecologically realistic conditions, or strong benefits in other conditions, at a higher rate than costly-and-dispensable genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: costly-conserved genes are clearly more often important in some other or ecologically realistic condition than costly-dispensable genes. Refute: the two groups look alike, or costly-conserved genes show no benefit anywhere, pointing to noise or drift.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 supplies the fitness data and 22761588 shows costly superfluous genes can be lost, but neither tests whether costly conserved genes have hidden benefits.
directions.question: Do genes that make mutants grow better in the lab yet stay conserved across a species' genomes carry benefits under field-like conditions that standard assays miss?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and pangenome tables are in the catalog; the robust burden classification and the cross-link must be computed, and ecological-condition tests need new assays.
directions.test: In the Fitness Browser, classify genes as costly using a replicate-robust criterion rather than one positive-fitness experiment. Join them to core versus accessory status from the pangenome gene clusters. Compare costly-conserved and costly-dispensable genes for strong negative fitness in any other condition, with focus on Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough field-stress and metal conditions. Then test a few candidates in soil or host-like media.
directions.title: Are costly-but-conserved genes kept by selection in natural conditions absent from laboratory assays?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, laboratory 'burden' labels overstate real gene cost and purifying selection can be inferred from conservation. If false, much conservation is inertia or trade-off without a benefit we can identify.

directions.hypothesis: Costly-dispensable genes are enriched for mobile-element context, such as neighbouring integrases, sparse distribution across genomes and singleton status, beyond what keyword annotation shows, and their loss rate exceeds that of costly-conserved genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: costly-dispensable genes sit near mobile-element genes and are patchy across genomes, including among unannotated genes. Refute: after domain search, a large share are ordinary metabolic genes with no mobile context.
directions.prior_work: 22448042 and 36097170 address gene loss and pangenome-dependent essentiality, but none tests the mobile-element origin of costly non-conserved genes.
directions.question: Do costly genes that are not conserved represent recently acquired horizontally transferred elements rather than decaying metabolic pathways?
directions.readiness_basis: All tables appear in the catalog, but genomic-context and domain analyses have not been run.
directions.test: Take costly-dispensable and costly-conserved genes from the Fitness Browser, link to pangenome clusters, and compare genomic neighbourhood, domain content (InterPro), singleton status and the fraction of species genomes carrying each cluster. Check unannotated genes by domain search for transposase or phage signatures.
directions.title: Are costly dispensable genes mostly recent mobile-element acquisitions still on their way to loss?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that most laboratory-detected burden reflects selfish elements in transit, not streamlining of metabolism, and would redirect studies of genome reduction.

directions.hypothesis: Core enrichment of metal-important genes comes from general stress and housekeeping functions; metal-specific genes with no other-stress phenotype are not more core than baseline, and the essential-versus-toxic gap disappears once gene detectability is matched.
directions.outcomes: Support: metal-specific genes show no core enrichment, or it vanishes after matching. Refute: enrichment stays for metal-specific genes after matching, as in 12 of 14 metals after shared-stress removal.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 25968644 provide the fitness assays and 12829273 describes efflux resistance, but none compares core status of metal-specific versus general stress genes.
directions.question: Why are genes needed under metal stress more often core, and more so for essential metals than toxic ones?
directions.readiness_basis: The metal experiments and core calls are in cataloged tables, and the matched regression has not been run.
directions.test: Across Fitness Browser organisms with metal experiments, define metal-specific genes (important under a metal, not under NaCl or other stresses), and compare their core fraction with baseline, per metal. Match core and accessory genes on annotation depth and fitness magnitude, and regress core status on magnitude and condition class together. Check whether the essential-versus-toxic difference survives.
directions.title: Does the core-genome enrichment of metal-stress genes reflect general stress robustness rather than metal-specific selection?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate niche-specific selection from general functional importance as the cause of conservation, and show how far metal tolerance can be predicted from the core genome.

directions.hypothesis: Per-metal lab tolerance, not an aggregate score, predicts the abundance ratio between high and low uranium sites once genus-level matching and geochemical covariates are included.
directions.outcomes: Support: per-metal scores track field abundance in the right direction after covariates. Refute: no relationship, or Caulobacter and Herbaspirillum directions contradict their lab scores.
directions.prior_work: 30523276 shows Rhodanobacter rising with uranium in this aquifer, but no work tests lab fitness as a predictor across genera.
directions.question: Can laboratory fitness under metal stress predict genus abundance across Oak Ridge sites with differing uranium?
directions.readiness_basis: Abundance, chemistry and fitness tables appear in the catalog; matching and covariate modelling remain undone, and the catalog did not show metadata linking every sample.
directions.test: Match Fitness Browser genera to Oak Ridge amplicon data, replace the aggregate score with per-metal fitness scores, and correlate with each site's uranium and metal concentrations, adding pH and oxygen as covariates. Compare Caulobacter (less abundant at high uranium) and Herbaspirillum (more abundant), and Desulfovibrio, which is too rare to test. Extend beyond 12 genera.
directions.title: Does lab-measured metal tolerance predict which genera thrive at uranium-contaminated field sites?
directions.why_it_matters: A working link would let lab fitness screens forecast field persistence. A failure would show lab fitness misses the selective pressures that structure natural communities.

directions.hypothesis: Random non-AMR genes matched on mean fitness show equal flagellar enrichment in their cofitness neighbourhoods, so the signal is a general feature of dispensable genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: matched controls reproduce the enrichment, and it does not rise under antibiotics. Refute: AMR genes stay uniquely enriched, and more so under antibiotic stress.
directions.prior_work: 31501286 links resistance regulators to flagellar repression in Salmonella, but no paper tests this across organisms against fitness-matched controls.
directions.question: Is the flagellar and biosynthesis enrichment among antimicrobial-resistance gene cofitness partners explained by shared dispensability in the lab?
directions.readiness_basis: Cofitness and fitness tables are in the catalog; the matched permutation has not been run.
directions.test: For organisms with the flagellar enrichment, draw random non-AMR genes matched on mean fitness and conservation class, compute cofitness neighbourhood GO enrichment, and compare with AMR genes. Compute cofitness separately for antibiotic versus standard conditions, and check whether flagellar knockouts have positive mean fitness.
directions.title: Do AMR cofitness partners reflect shared dispensability rather than regulatory coupling?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether cofitness networks of resistance genes encode biology or lab artefacts, affecting how cofitness is used for resistance gene function.

directions.hypothesis: Most xoxF-positive Acidobacteriota and Gemmatimonadota genomes carry PQQ synthesis genes and other lanthanide-cassette genes at rates similar to canonical methylotroph families. Genomes lacking them show signs of fragmented assembly or truncated genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: cassette completeness in these phyla is similar to the reference families, and gaps track low genome quality. Refute: the cassette is mostly absent even in high-quality genomes, so xoxF calls there do not indicate lanthanide use.
directions.prior_work: The retrieved papers (34739369, 34597405, 32341564) are annotation and taxonomy tools and report no xoxF rates by phylum, so this goes beyond them by testing whether the calls reflect a full cassette.
directions.question: Acidobacteriota and Gemmatimonadota show high per-genome xoxF rates, yet they are rarely cited in methylotrophy work. Do these genomes carry the PQQ synthesis genes and other lanthanide-associated genes that would indicate real lanthanide-dependent methanol oxidation?
directions.readiness_basis: The annotation and taxonomy tables appear in the catalog, but per-genome cassette scoring and gene-neighbourhood analysis must be run.
directions.test: In the KBase Data Lakehouse pangenome, list genomes with xoxF (eggNOG K00114) in Acidobacteriota, Gemmatimonadota and Beijerinckiaceae/Hyphomicrobiaceae as reference. Score each for PQQ synthesis genes and neighbouring genes using eggNOG and Bakta annotations, gene order on the genome, and genome completeness from the GTDB metadata. Compare cassette completeness between phyla.
directions.title: Do xoxF-carrying Acidobacteriota and Gemmatimonadota also hold the rest of a lanthanide-use cassette?
directions.why_it_matters: If the cassette is intact, xoxF calls in these phyla would be candidate lanthanide-using methanol oxidizers, a possible extension of lanthanide-dependent methanol oxidation to new phyla pending functional validation. If not, the high rates reflect over-calling of a broad enzyme family.

directions.hypothesis: The 13 lanmodulin-without-xoxF genomes differ from the other 49 in carrying other lanthanide-associated genes, or in having low genome completeness, rather than being random annotation misses.
directions.outcomes: Support: the 13 carry distinct neighbouring genes, or show no xoxF even with sensitive search in complete genomes. Refute: sensitive search recovers xoxF in most of the 13, or they are mostly incomplete genomes, which points to annotation gaps.
directions.prior_work: The retrieved papers (34739369, 34597405) describe annotation tools, not lanmodulin, so this goes beyond them by asking what the xoxF-free lanmodulin genomes carry.
directions.question: Lanmodulin occurs only in three alpha-proteobacterial methylotroph families, and 13 of 62 lanmodulin genomes lack xoxF. Are these missed xoxF calls, or do they use another lanthanide-handling system?
directions.readiness_basis: The 62 genomes were already identified and the annotation tables are in the catalog; the sequence search and neighbourhood comparison still need to be run.
directions.test: Take the 62 Bakta-validated lanmodulin genomes. For the 13 without xoxF, search the genome sequences for xoxF-like genes by sequence similarity, and compare genome completeness and gene neighbourhoods around lanmodulin with those in the 49 xoxF-positive genomes. Use eggNOG and Bakta annotations and GTDB metadata in the pangenome.
directions.title: Do lanmodulin genomes lacking xoxF use an alternative lanthanide-handling route?
directions.why_it_matters: The co-occurrence of lanmodulin and xoxF fell just under the pre-set 80% threshold. Resolving the 13 genomes would show whether lanmodulin has a role apart from methanol dehydrogenase.

directions.hypothesis: mxaF is clustered in a small number of families, and within most families that carry either gene xoxF outnumbers mxaF, so the pooled ratio understates xoxF dominance within typical lineages.
directions.outcomes: Support: mxaF is confined to few families and xoxF outnumbers it in most mixed families, in both models. Refute: mxaF is spread widely, or the ratio varies sharply by family and the modelled ratio depends on the random-effect structure.
directions.prior_work: The retrieved papers (32341564, 34597405) provide taxonomy and annotation but no xoxF or mxaF distribution, so this goes beyond them by locating the excess across lineages.
directions.question: The pooled xoxF to mxaF ratio is about 19 to 1, while a model with phylum and family effects gives about 143 to 1. Where does mxaF sit across lineages, and does xoxF dominance hold within families?
directions.readiness_basis: The ratio was already computed from these annotation and taxonomy tables; the new family-level modelling needs to be run.
directions.test: Using the GTDB r214 pangenome, tabulate xoxF (K00114) and mxaF (K14028) carriage per family. Compare the model with family effects against a version that also adds genus, and compare ratios in families with both genes. Re-run excluding xoxF genomes with low completeness.
directions.title: Does xoxF dominance over mxaF persist inside individual phyla, or is mxaF concentrated in a few lineages?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether the xoxF excess is a broad pattern across lineages or driven by a few large groups. That would shape which taxa to target when searching for calcium-dependent versus lanthanide-dependent methanol oxidizers.

directions.hypothesis: xoxF-bearing genomes are more common in rare-earth-impacted metagenomes than in matched non-impacted samples from the same phyla, whereas lanmodulin stays rare.
directions.outcomes: Support: a higher within-phylum xoxF rate in rare-earth-impacted samples. Refute: rates match those of other environments. The catalog did not show whether enough such samples exist in the lakehouse, so too few samples would leave the question open.
directions.prior_work: The retrieved papers (34739369, 32341564) are tools and do not address rare-earth environments, so this adds an environment comparison.
directions.question: Only 4 of 37 rare-earth acid mine drainage MAGs carry any xoxF and none carry lanmodulin. Does a larger collection of rare-earth-impacted metagenomes show a higher xoxF rate than comparable sites without rare-earth enrichment?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog lists biosample and MAG tables but does not show how many rare-earth-impacted samples or MAG annotations they hold.
directions.test: Find rare-earth-impacted samples (mining tailings, leachate, bioreactors) using biosample attributes and NMDC metadata. Count xoxF and lanmodulin in their MAGs, and compare with MAGs from other environments within the same phyla, using a model with phylum and family effects.
directions.title: Does rare-earth supply select for the xoxF cassette in rare-earth-impacted metagenomes?
directions.why_it_matters: The small drainage set can only describe. A larger comparison would show whether rare-earth availability is linked to xoxF carriage in nature or whether the gene's spread is independent of the environment.

directions.hypothesis: Adding reactions for the quinate-specific genes the model cannot map, including PQQ and iron supply steps, will make the model predict Complex I as more needed on quinate than on glucose.
directions.outcomes: Support: predicted Complex I essentiality rises on quinate relative to glucose after the additions, in line with measured ratios. Refute: predicted essentiality stays near zero after the additions, or rises equally on acetate and succinate, where measured Complex I defects are also large.
directions.prior_work: The ADP1 deletion collection (18319726) and the succinate-to-quinate multiomics study (25374488) cover the organism and substrates but not Complex I essentiality or model blind spots.
directions.question: In Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1, Complex I is more essential on quinate than on glucose or acetate even though quinate gives fewer NADH per carbon, and flux balance analysis predicts no Complex I essentiality. Which model gaps explain the mismatch?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows the reaction table and Fitness Browser tables; the ADP1 model and growth data were not shown, so the model rerun needs compute.
directions.test: Take the 30 of 51 quinate-specific ADP1 genes with no reaction mapping. Add reactions for the PQQ and iron supply steps and for known regulators as constraints, using the ModelSEED reaction table. Rerun the model on quinate, glucose and acetate and compare predicted Complex I essentiality with the measured growth ratios. Then compare with ortholog-transferred Complex I fitness in the Fitness Browser on aromatic versus non-aromatic conditions. Follow with single-organism growth tests of Complex I and PQQ-pathway mutants on quinate if the model is improved.
directions.title: Why does Complex I matter most on quinate when metabolic models predict no need?
directions.why_it_matters: If the mismatch comes from missing cofactor-supply and regulatory content, model-based essentiality calls on aromatic substrates can be repaired. If not, the cause lies outside the network structure.

directions.hypothesis: Pathway completeness calculated from expressed transcripts shows a stronger negative link to ambient amino acid intensity than completeness calculated from taxonomic gene content.
directions.outcomes: Support: the expression-based measure gives a clearly stronger negative association for leucine and arginine. Refute: the two measures agree or the expression measure is weaker. Most current samples come from one study, so cross-study agreement should be reported.
directions.prior_work: Studies 31316056, 33311510 and 35085485 link communities to metabolites by prediction or ecological modelling, but not through pathway completeness and ambient amino acids.
directions.question: Community completeness of amino acid biosynthesis pathways tends to fall as the ambient amino acid rises in NMDC soil samples. Does the signal come from expressed pathways rather than gene presence?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog lists NMDC metabolomics, file and taxonomy tables, but the shown columns do not confirm which samples have expression data.
directions.test: For NMDC samples with paired metabolomics, compute leucine and arginine pathway completeness two ways: from taxonomy profiles (Kraken, Centrifuge, contig rollups) linked to GapMind pathway calls, and from metatranscriptome-derived abundances where files exist. Compare each against ambient metabolite intensity from the metabolomics table.
directions.title: Does expressed pathway completeness explain Black Queen-type amino acid signals in soil metabolomes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether the Black Queen pattern reflects active gene use in communities. That would justify expression-based metabolic ecology over genome-based prediction.

directions.hypothesis: Tryptophan release by FW300-N2E3 supports growth of a tryptophan-requiring partner, and the strain's tryptophan genes are biosynthetic or regulatory, not catabolic.
directions.outcomes: Support: tryptophan genes are mostly biosynthetic or regulatory, and the auxotroph grows on spent medium in proportion to the tryptophan released. Refute: the strain's fitness depends on catabolic genes, or spent medium does not support the auxotroph.
directions.prior_work: The Web of Microbes paper (30208844) describes the exometabolomics resource but reports no tryptophan overflow or exchange role for this strain.
directions.question: FW300-N2E3 produces tryptophan and grows on it as sole carbon source, yet the species as a whole cannot catabolize it. Does the excreted tryptophan serve other cells?
directions.readiness_basis: The gene mapping can use catalog tables, but the cross-feeding test needs new growth experiments.
directions.test: Run the deferred step: map FW300-N2E3 fitness genes to GapMind tryptophan pathway steps and classify them as biosynthetic, catabolic or regulatory, using Fitness Browser and Web of Microbes data. Compare BacDive tryptophan use across the P. fluorescens group. Then grow a tryptophan auxotroph with FW300-N2E3 spent medium or in coculture and measure growth.
directions.title: Is tryptophan overflow in Pseudomonas FW300-N2E3 a cross-feeding signal rather than waste?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that production-versus-use mismatches in exometabolomics point to exchange. Such mismatches could then guide community design.

directions.hypothesis: D. vulgaris has lost serine synthesis and relies on environmental serine, so it will not grow without serine and no divergent homolog of the canonical enzymes will be found.
directions.outcomes: Support: no candidate enzyme is found, the gap is shared across the species, and growth needs serine. Refute: a divergent enzyme is found or growth occurs without serine, which would mean annotation failure.
directions.prior_work: The D. vulgaris genome (15077118) and mutant phenotype study (29769716) do not address serine loss; GapMind (32576650) supplies the pathway calls tested here.
directions.question: Desulfovibrio vulgaris is the only one of seven organisms lacking a complete serine pathway by GapMind. Is serine synthesis truly lost, or does it use divergent enzymes?
directions.readiness_basis: Homology search uses catalog tables, but the growth test needs new cultures.
directions.test: Search D. vulgaris proteins for divergent homologs of serine biosynthesis enzymes using eggNOG annotations and curated PaperBLAST genes. Check the pangenome for the same gap across Desulfovibrio genomes. Test growth in defined medium with and without serine.
directions.title: Is apparent serine auxotrophy in Desulfovibrio vulgaris genomic economy or a missed pathway?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate real gene loss from annotation gaps in pathway-based prototrophy calls. It would also bear on whether prototrophy is the usual state in free-living bacteria.

directions.hypothesis: If Black Queen gene loss drives the pattern, the negative link between pathway completeness and ambient amino acid should hold across independent studies and sit mainly in costly pathways. If consumption drives it, the link should vanish once community uptake capacity is accounted for.
directions.outcomes: Support: negative slopes in most studies, and they persist after the uptake covariate. Refute: slopes that are near zero or that change sign across studies, or that vanish after the uptake covariate. The current signal comes almost entirely from one soil study, so failure to replicate is a real possibility.
directions.prior_work: The papers (35085485, 31316056, 33311510) link communities to metabolites by prediction or ecological modelling, and 24910088 argues for selective loss of biosynthetic genes. None tests a Black Queen pattern against measured ambient amino acids across studies.
directions.question: Do communities lose amino acid biosynthesis capacity where the amino acid is freely available, or does the negative link between completeness and ambient amino acid reflect something else, such as consumption of the amino acid?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows NMDC metabolomics, taxonomy and GapMind tables, but the genus-to-pathway bridge and the per-study splits still have to be computed.
directions.test: Using NMDC paired taxonomy and metabolomics, score leucine, arginine and the other testable amino acid pathways from genus-level GapMind completeness in the pangenome. Regress completeness on ambient intensity separately in each NMDC study, adding a covariate for the community's amino acid uptake or catabolism genes. Compare pathways by biosynthetic cost. Add a held-out study not used for the first signal.
directions.title: Does community amino acid biosynthesis completeness fall where ambient amino acids are abundant, as Black Queen dynamics predict?
directions.why_it_matters: A community-level signature of gene loss from public goods would show that auxotrophy is shaped by the local chemical environment, not only by lineage. That would change how cross-feeding dependence is predicted from metagenomes.

directions.hypothesis: Pathways whose completeness depends on accessory genes are more often fitness-neutral than pathways completed by core genes, and this accounts for most of the link between latent fraction and pangenome openness.
directions.outcomes: Support: accessory-dependent pathways are more often neutral, and the openness link shrinks once they are modelled. Refute: no difference between the groups, or an openness link that stays unchanged. Latent pathways were not separated from active ones by how conserved they are, so a refutation is likely to be informative.
directions.prior_work: 24910088 explains biosynthetic gene loss and 32589566 compares amino acid pathways within one genus. Neither separates core-dependent from accessory-dependent pathways to explain the openness trend.
directions.question: Do species with open pangenomes keep more complete but dispensable pathways because those pathways sit in accessory genes that are gained and lost, or does the link reflect uneven fitness testing?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows the fitness, pathway and gene-cluster tables, but linking pathway steps to core or accessory clusters is a new computation.
directions.test: For Fitness Browser organisms, label each complete pathway as core-only or accessory-dependent from the pangenome gene clusters and GapMind steps. Compare the share of fitness-neutral pathways between the two groups within species. Then test whether the openness link remains after the accessory-dependent share is added to the model. Control for the number of conditions tested per organism.
directions.title: Does the latent share of complete pathways rise with pangenome openness because accessory genes supply them?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that dispensable metabolism is a feature of how open genomes are structured. That would make auxotrophy and pathway loss predictable from pangenome structure.

directions.hypothesis: D. vulgaris Hildenborough cannot grow without serine in defined medium, and its fitness data show serine uptake genes that matter only when serine is scarce. An alternative is a divergent enzyme route that GapMind misses.
directions.outcomes: Support: no growth without serine, rescue by serine or a partner, and no alternative pathway in the fitness data. Refute: growth without serine, or fitness defects in a candidate non-canonical route.
directions.prior_work: 15077118 gives the genome and 29769716 the mutant fitness data. 24910088 proposes an economy explanation for gene loss in general, but none tests serine in this organism.
directions.question: Is Desulfovibrio vulgaris truly unable to make serine, and if so, is the loss an economy that depends on serine being supplied?
directions.readiness_basis: Growth tests on serine-free medium are not in the catalog, and the pathway calls come from only 7 organisms.
directions.test: Grow D. vulgaris on serine-free and serine-supplied defined media with and without cross-feeding partners. Check lower-confidence GapMind calls and fitness profiles for serine-related genes in the Fitness Browser. If it grows without serine, run isotope labelling to trace the route.
directions.title: Does serine auxotrophy in Desulfovibrio vulgaris reflect genomic economy rather than an unrecognised pathway?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate real auxotrophy from annotation gaps in a model sulfate reducer. It would also add a worked example of gene loss in a free-living bacterium.

directions.hypothesis: Acinetobacter and Aeromonas isolates from the labile-carbon enrichment grow on the labile carbon but not on lignin-derived aromatics alone, whereas the lignin-only Pseudomonas isolates grow on aromatics alone.
directions.outcomes: Support: Acinetobacter and Aeromonas fail on aromatics alone but grow in co-culture with Pseudomonas. Refute: they grow on aromatics alone, which would make them direct degraders.
directions.prior_work: The papers (14614618, 29169786, 41045130) cover lignocellulose consortia and labile versus recalcitrant carbon. None tests whether the taxa that expand with labile carbon use aromatics themselves.
directions.question: When labile carbon is added to a lignin enrichment, do Acinetobacter and Aeromonas grow on the labile carbon alone while Pseudomonas and other specialists decline, and does this alter community dependence?
directions.readiness_basis: Isolates and growth assays are not in the catalog, and the original enrichments had only 3 replicates per group.
directions.test: Isolate Acinetobacter, Aeromonas and Pseudomonas from the lignin-only and lignin plus labile-carbon enrichments. Test growth on lignin-derived aromatics alone, labile carbon alone, and both. Run pairwise co-cultures to look for cross-feeding. Use at least 6 replicate enrichments, since the original had 3 per group.
directions.title: Does adding labile carbon to a lignin enrichment make aromatic degraders depend on cross-feeding?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether the copiotroph shift is a change in who uses the lignin carbon or only in who uses the added sugar. That affects how enrichments are used to find lignin degraders.

directions.hypothesis: Soil species that lack tryptophan synthesis but carry ipdC also carry tryptophan uptake genes or TyrR, so ipdC use depends on scavenged tryptophan.
directions.outcomes: Support: trp-incomplete ipdC carriers are enriched for uptake genes or TyrR beyond what genome size predicts. Refute: no enrichment, or a reversal that disappears when genome size or lineage is controlled. The soil reversal is hypothesis-generating, and ipdC is carried by few species.
directions.prior_work: 18757531 shows tryptophan induces ipdC through TyrR in one strain, and 40130845 covers ipdC physiology. Neither tests species-level links between tryptophan supply and ipdC.
directions.question: Why are tryptophan-complete soil species less likely to carry ipdC, and does exudate-supplied tryptophan explain it?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows the pangenome pathway, annotation and environment tables, and the covariate model still has to be run.
directions.test: In the pangenome, split species by tryptophan completeness and environment. Test ipdC carriage against tryptophan transporter genes and TyrR, adding genome size and total complete pathways as covariates. Repeat within genera to control for lineage.
directions.title: Does tryptophan completeness predict ipdC carriage in soil species through root-exudate tryptophan supply?
directions.why_it_matters: It would link auxotrophy to plant-growth-promoting traits. Dependence on host-supplied amino acids would then help explain which soil bacteria make auxin.

directions.hypothesis: Costly dispensable genes are concentrated in rare, recently gained gene clusters (singleton or low-prevalence). The few metabolic genes among them show no more loss than matched metabolic genes, so the set mostly reflects gene gain rather than adaptive loss.
directions.outcomes: Support: costly dispensable genes are strongly enriched in rare clusters and the metabolic remainder is small and no more lost than controls. Refute: a sizable metabolic group is lost in related genomes. Even then it would only be a gene-loss pattern until a provider test links it to the Black Queen idea.
directions.prior_work: 22448042 and 22761588 describe adaptive and selection-driven gene loss, and 29769716 supplies the fitness data. None tests the age or mobility of costly dispensable genes.
directions.question: Genes that burden growth in the lab yet are absent from many relatives are mostly mobile-element genes. Are they young arrivals that selection has not yet purged, or do they include metabolic genes whose loss pattern points to adaptive loss?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows fitness, cluster-status and annotation tables, but linking Fitness Browser genes to pangenome clusters needs a new join.
directions.test: For Fitness Browser organisms, link each costly dispensable and costly conserved gene to its pangenome cluster. Compare cluster prevalence and singleton share, and annotate mobile versus metabolic content with Bakta annotations. For the metabolic remainder, describe the loss pattern across close relatives only as a gene-loss pattern. Calling it Black Queen loss would need community or provider-presence data, so test whether relatives lacking the gene co-occur with others carrying it.
directions.title: Are costly but dispensable genes mostly recently acquired mobile elements rather than eroding metabolic pathways?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether lab-measured gene burden mainly reflects horizontal acquisition of selfish elements. That would narrow which genes can be treated as candidates for adaptive gene loss, which would additionally need evidence that a partner supplies the function.

directions.hypothesis: Costly conserved genes are more likely than other core genes to show a strong fitness defect in at least one other tested condition, which fits selection maintaining them for conditions outside the burden-scoring experiments.
directions.outcomes: Support: costly conserved genes have more conditional defects than matched core genes. Refute: they look like matched core genes or defects are absent, which would point to noise or trade-offs without a benefit.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 22761588 give the fitness data and gene-cost concept. They do not test whether costly conserved genes carry benefits in other conditions.
directions.question: Thousands of core genes burden growth in lab conditions yet stay conserved. Do they carry fitness benefits under other conditions, or is the burden a measurement artifact?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and pangenome tables are in the catalog, but per-gene fitness values and the cluster join were not shown, so compute is needed.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser data, define costly conserved genes (burden in some experiment, core in the pangenome). Compare them with matched core genes, matched on functional category such as RNA metabolism, on whether they have strong defects in other experiments and on how many condition classes show defects. Require a burden in at least two independent experiments, to guard against single-experiment noise. Include the cell wall category, where non-core genes were more burdensome.
directions.title: Do costly but conserved genes matter in conditions the lab never tested?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate true conditional essentiality from noise in burden calls and show how much of the conserved genome the standard lab conditions miss.

directions.hypothesis: Pathway variability tracks openness mainly because incomplete pathways are completed by accessory genes. The link stays after controlling for genus, and it is stronger for accessory genes with mobile-element context than for other accessory genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: the link persists within genera and is stronger for mobile-context accessory genes. Refute: it disappears within genera, pointing to phylogeny and sampling depth.
directions.prior_work: 31639358 and 38743630 relate pangenomes to lifestyle, and 41961409 studies openness in Bacillus. None asks which accessory gene types complete variable pathways.
directions.question: Species with more variable metabolic pathways have more open pangenomes. Are the variable pathways completed by accessory genes of mobile origin, or by ordinary accessory genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway, cluster and annotation tables are in the catalog, but the genome-to-cluster pathway completion mapping needs computing.
directions.test: Using GapMind pathway calls per genome and cluster status, find species where pathway completeness depends on accessory clusters. Use Bakta annotations for mobile context. Fit pathway variability against openness with controls for genome count and genus, then split by accessory-gene type. Compare against AMR count, whose overall link with openness was near zero.
directions.title: Is the link between pathway variability and pangenome openness carried by accessory mobile genes?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether metabolic variation in open pangenomes comes from gene exchange or from within-lineage diversification, and whether openness is a metabolic trait or a sampling effect.

directions.hypothesis: Prophage density predicts AMR breadth less within genera than across species. Once openness and environmental diversity are controlled, the association shrinks sharply, which would favor shared open-pangenome effects over phage-driven transfer.
directions.outcomes: Support: the prophage term stays large within genera after controls. Refute: it drops near zero once openness and environment enter.
directions.prior_work: 30576310 links prophages and resistance to capsules and larger pangenomes. 30453138, 26078016 and 33980677 show phage-associated transfer. None separates prophage density from openness and environment.
directions.question: Species with denser prophages carry broader AMR repertoires, yet the association reverses at very close range. Does prophage density add information beyond pangenome openness and environment?
directions.readiness_basis: AMR, annotation, pangenome and environment tables are listed, but the species-level aggregation and gene-neighborhood analysis need new computation.
directions.test: Per species, compute prophage-like gene density from Bakta annotation keywords (the catalog did not show dedicated prophage calls), AMR breadth from the Bakta AMR table, openness from cluster counts and environmental diversity from AlphaEarth embeddings. Fit nested models with genus as a grouping term and compare the prophage term. Also repeat the gene-distance analysis separately for core and accessory AMR clusters.
directions.title: Does prophage density predict AMR breadth beyond shared open-pangenome effects?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether prophages are a general route for resistance spread or both traits just accumulate in open, ecologically diverse species. That affects how surveillance uses prophage content.

directions.hypothesis: Genes important for only one metal or a few metals are less core than genes important across many stresses, so the core enrichment comes from general stress genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: core fraction is highest for general genes and near baseline for metal-specific genes. Refute: metal-specific genes are as core-enriched as general genes, or more so.
directions.prior_work: 29769716 and 25968644 supply the fitness method, and 12829273 and 24304895 catalog metal resistance. None splits core enrichment by metal-specific versus general stress genes.
directions.question: Genes with fitness defects under metal stress are more often core than baseline. Is this because they are general stress-response genes, or do metal-specific genes also sit in the core?
directions.readiness_basis: Fitness and cluster tables are in the catalog, but the per-gene specificity scores and gene-to-cluster join need computing.
directions.test: In Fitness Browser data for the 22 organisms and 14 metals, score each gene by how many unrelated stress experiments (non-metal) and metal experiments show a defect. Compare core fraction for metal-specific, metal-plus-general, and general-only genes against baseline, separating essential from toxic metals. Use pangenome cluster status from the species clades.
directions.title: Is metal-stress fitness enrichment in core genes driven by general stress genes?
