directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether specific metal tolerance is a core trait or an accessory one, which affects predicting tolerance from genomes. The earlier broad definition of metal-important genes limits that inference now.

directions.hypothesis: Costly dispensable genes are mostly recent acquisitions inside prophage or transposon regions, so they are accessory, patchily distributed across the species, and near other mobile genes more often than costly conserved genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: costly dispensable genes cluster near mobile genes and are singleton or accessory far more often, in most species. Refute: after matching for annotation, proximity and patchiness do not differ, or enrichment disappears when one-experiment burden calls are replaced by repeated-experiment calls.
directions.prior_work: 22448042 and 36097170 treat gene loss and pangenome essentiality, but not whether burden genes are mobile-element debris; this tests their position and age directly.
directions.question: Do costly-but-dispensable genes in Fitness Browser organisms sit on recently acquired mobile elements, and are they older or younger than costly conserved genes?
directions.readiness_basis: Both datasets are in the catalog, but linking genes to clusters and computing gene neighbourhoods needs new joins.
directions.test: Link Fitness Browser genes with max fitness above 1 to pangenome clusters. Compare costly+dispensable and costly+conserved genes for neighbour distance to transposase, integrase and phage genes, accessory or singleton status, and GC deviation, within each species. Use COG L and V annotations as a cross-check.
directions.title: Are costly but dispensable genes mostly horizontally acquired mobile elements still awaiting loss?
directions.why_it_matters: If true, genome expansion by horizontal transfer, not decaying metabolism, is the main source of burden genes, and gene loss is a slow clean-up of selfish DNA.

directions.hypothesis: Prophage density predicts AMR breadth through a shared taxon-level propensity for gene uptake, not phage-mediated transfer, so AMR genes are no more often next to complete prophages than matched non-AMR accessory genes.
directions.outcomes: Support: after matching, AMR genes are not closer to prophages and the scaling falls once uptake propensity is included. Refute: AMR genes are closer to complete prophages than matched accessory genes in many species, including at close range.
directions.prior_work: 30576310 and 30453138 link resistance genes to prophages and capsules; this adds matched accessory controls and the close-range reversal.
directions.question: Is the scaling of AMR breadth with prophage density caused by phage-linked transfer, or by a shared tendency of some species to take up foreign DNA?
directions.readiness_basis: AMR, cluster and annotation tables are in the catalog; the matched-control distance analysis is not yet run.
directions.test: Per species, use AMR gene calls and prophage annotations from the pangenome. Compare AMR-to-prophage distance with distance for accessory genes matched on cluster frequency, at several distance cut-offs including very close range. Add pangenome openness, which had near zero overall correlation with AMR count, as a covariate. Fit within-phylum models.
directions.title: Does prophage load drive AMR breadth, or do open pangenomes accumulate both independently?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate phage-borne spread of resistance from a general permissiveness to foreign DNA, which implies different interventions.

directions.hypothesis: Part of the universal positive association comes from defense systems carried inside or beside prophages; it weakens when prophage-embedded systems are removed.
directions.outcomes: Support: the association drops sharply after exclusion and pairs sit in islands. Refute: it stays similar in all phyla and defense genes are mostly outside prophages.
directions.prior_work: 29371424 and 29085076 describe defense islands; this tests whether the pan-phylum link with prophage burden reflects defense carried by prophages.
directions.question: Why does defense-system count rise with prophage burden in every major phylum, and are the defense systems encoded within the prophages themselves?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotations are in the catalog, but defense-prophage positional analysis needs new computation.
directions.test: In species from the pangenome, locate defense genes, including R-M Type II, Gabija and CBASS, relative to prophage regions. Recompute the within-phylum partial association between defense count and prophage burden, controlling for genome size, after excluding defense genes within prophage boundaries. Test whether Gabija and R-M co-occurring pairs sit together on the genome.
directions.title: Does defense-system richness track prophage burden because defenses guard against, or are carried by, prophages?
directions.why_it_matters: It would distinguish an arms-race explanation from mobile-element hitchhiking of defense genes, reshaping how defense repertoires are interpreted.

directions.hypothesis: Tail, head and anti-defense modules from human-associated genomes have phylogenies discordant with their terminase lineage and host phylogeny, showing modular exchange.
directions.outcomes: Support: modules are discordant with TerL and host trees more than expected, and human-associated enrichment survives controls. Refute: module trees match TerL lineage, or enrichment vanishes with finer taxon strata or depth control.
directions.prior_work: 35746669 and 28692019 show phage module mosaicism; this ties it to environment with a lineage-level null.
directions.question: Are environmental differences in prophage content due to modules or anti-defense genes being exchanged between unrelated prophages?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotations and isolation metadata are in the catalog; trees and incongruence tests need computing, and metadata are sparse.
directions.test: Build trees for tail, head and anti-defense modules and the TerL marker across genomes from human-associated and other isolation sources. Test incongruence with host and TerL trees. Compare human-associated versus other environments with genus-level controls and sampling-depth controls.
directions.title: Do prophage modules move between hosts independently of the phage lineage that carries them?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that environment selects phage parts, not whole phages, which affects how phage ecology is modeled.

directions.hypothesis: Mechanism differences in conservation reflect origin (intrinsic chromosomal versus mobile acquisition), not cost, so accessory efflux and enzymatic genes sit near mobile elements and core ones sit in the chromosomal backbone.
directions.outcomes: Support: mobile proximity absorbs the mechanism effect on conservation while cost stays flat. Refute: mechanism still predicts conservation after proximity and phylum are included, or cost differs by origin.
directions.prior_work: 25861385 and 20208551 cover costs of resistance; this asks why conservation, not cost, separates mechanisms.
directions.question: If mechanism does not predict lab fitness cost, what explains the strong mechanism differences in core versus accessory status?
directions.readiness_basis: AMR and cluster tables are in the catalog; linking to fitness and neighbours needs new joins.
directions.test: For AMR clusters in Fitness Browser species, classify mechanism, core or accessory status, and distance to mobile genes. Fit a joint model of core status on mechanism, mobile proximity and phylum. Check whether cost differs between recent accessory and long-resident core genes, restricting to species with over 20 genomes.
directions.title: Why do resistance genes show no fitness cost by mechanism yet differ in conservation by mechanism?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show that selection or mobility, not lab cost, shapes resistome structure, and that intrinsic and acquired labels can be measured.

directions.hypothesis: After matching species for genome count and phylogeny and reweighting for sampling intensity, the clinical excess in AMR clusters shrinks sharply but does not vanish, because some of the excess is real selection and some is sampling preference.
directions.outcomes: Support: the clinical excess falls but remains in matched, equal-depth comparisons. Refute: it disappears at equal depth within genus, meaning the original difference was sampling preference.
directions.prior_work: 25003965 and 22936781 show resistomes cluster by ecology and overlap between soil and pathogens; this direction asks whether the clinical excess in per-species counts survives equal-depth, within-genus comparison.
directions.question: Do clinical species really carry more antimicrobial resistance (AMR) gene clusters, or do clinical species simply get sequenced more deeply and because of their resistance?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows AMR gene calls, biome labels, environment metadata and species clades; the join and subsampling need new compute, and the catalog did not show per-genome clinical labels directly.
directions.test: Using AMR gene calls in the MGnify genome catalogue and the pangenome species table with NCBI environment metadata, compute per-species AMR cluster counts. Compare clinical and soil, aquatic or host species within the same genus, subsample every species to equal genome numbers, and repeat after excluding genomes from outbreak-style bioprojects. Also test whether clinical fraction still predicts accessory AMR share after this control.
directions.title: Does sequencing preference for clinical isolates explain why clinical species carry more AMR gene clusters?
directions.why_it_matters: Resistome comparisons across habitats underpin risk assessments of environmental reservoirs. If the clinical excess is mostly sampling, environmental species are underrated as AMR carriers; if it persists, clinical selection is real.

directions.hypothesis: Most top hotspots, including Atacama, are dominated by one or two bioprojects, and after weighting by project the regional enrichment falls to the level of nearby regions.
directions.outcomes: Support: leave-one-project-out removes or halves hotspot enrichment. Refute: enrichment stays across several independent projects in the cell.
directions.prior_work: 38886447 and 36473884 report metal resistance genes in soil and aquatic genomes; neither tests whether regional hotspots persist after controlling for study.
directions.question: Are the geographic hotspots of metal resistance among environmental MAGs (metagenome-assembled genomes), such as Atacama/Andean Chile, real regional signals or the output of single expeditions?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog shows coordinates, bioproject fields and environment attributes; the table holding MAG-level metal-resistance calls was not shown in the catalog and would need to be located or computed.
directions.test: Take MAGs with coordinates and link them to bioproject and environment metadata through the pangenome embedding table and NCBI environment attributes. For each hotspot cell count distinct bioprojects, then re-estimate enrichment with genomes grouped by project and with leave-one-project-out resampling. Compare Atacama (21.8% prevalence, n=101 MAGs) with matched cells.
directions.title: Is the Atacama metal-resistance hotspot a property of the place or of a single study?
directions.why_it_matters: Marine depletion and soil enrichment of metal resistance are used to infer where metals shape communities. If hotspots are study artefacts, biogeographic claims need project-aware analysis and targeted resampling.

directions.hypothesis: The contamination-site shift is mostly a taxonomic composition effect; within the same orders, contaminated-site isolates do not differ from environmental isolates beyond noise.
directions.outcomes: Support: the within-order difference is near zero while the pooled difference stays near one standard deviation. Refute: a clear within-order shift remains with adequate group sizes.
directions.prior_work: 37290750 compares genotype with measured tolerance in two species; this direction asks how much isolation site adds beyond lineage across BacDive.
directions.question: Do isolates from heavy-metal-contaminated sites truly carry higher genome-predicted metal tolerance once taxonomy is accounted for, given that taxonomy already explains much of the score?
directions.readiness_basis: The catalog showed only the BacDive isolation table; BacDive phenotype tables and the metal-score table were not shown, so feasibility depends on locating them.
directions.test: Using BacDive isolation categories, build contamination and baseline groups across the full database rather than the 10 matched isolates, and compare scores within order or class strata with a mixed model. Phenotype and metal-score tables were not shown in the catalog, so locate them first. Add a sample-size calculation per stratum before testing.
directions.title: Does the high metal-tolerance score of contamination-site isolates survive adequate sample size and taxonomic matching?
directions.why_it_matters: Genome-based tolerance scores are used to prioritise strains for bioremediation. If taxonomy absorbs the signal, isolation site adds no information and scores should be treated as lineage traits.

directions.hypothesis: The negative association holds in at least several independent studies with similar direction once study is a random effect; if it reflects one cohort, it vanishes.
directions.outcomes: Support: same-sign effect in most studies and in the pooled mixed model. Refute: the effect appears only in the original study or reverses elsewhere.
directions.prior_work: 31316056, 35085485 and 33311510 link communities to metabolites by prediction or modelling; none tests this leucine association across studies.
directions.question: Is communities' leucine-pathway completeness lower where ambient leucine is higher in general, as a Black Queen-style cross-feeding signal, or only in one study?
directions.readiness_basis: Catalog shows metabolomics, taxonomy, file-to-sample mapping and study tables; the number of studies with paired data was not shown.
directions.test: Match NMDC metabolomics features with taxonomy profiles by sample across all studies having both, compute pathway completeness per community, and fit leucine intensity against completeness with study as a random effect and leave-one-study-out checks. Compare leucine with arginine and with pathways showing no expected relation.
directions.title: Does the negative link between leucine biosynthesis completeness and ambient leucine hold across independent NMDC studies?
directions.why_it_matters: A reproducible link would show that environmental metabolite pools shape which community members keep biosynthesis genes, a prediction about gene loss under cross-feeding.

directions.hypothesis: Genome size and lineage absorb much of the gradient, but a smaller habitat effect remains between soil/plant and animal species within the same families.
directions.outcomes: Support: a habitat difference remains within families after genome-size control. Refute: the difference vanishes or reverses, as for niche breadth.
directions.prior_work: 14973198 links gene content to genome size and 37076457 covers soil carbon storage; neither tests PHB prevalence by habitat with genome size controlled.
directions.question: Is the environmental gradient in PHB capacity a habitat effect, or a by-product of genome size and lineage, as genome size already reversed the niche-breadth association?
directions.readiness_basis: Catalog shows genome metadata, pangenome sizes and environment tables; PHB gene-call tables were not shown and would need to be located.
directions.test: Join species PHB status to genome size and environment labels using the pangenome and GTDB metadata, and fit within-family models of PHB presence on environment with genome size as covariate. Repeat on species with embedding-derived environment (28% of genomes) versus all, to test coverage bias, and treat the 34.9% unknown-environment species as a sensitivity group.
directions.title: Does the PHB prevalence gradient across habitats persist after controlling for genome size and lineage?
directions.why_it_matters: It would decide whether carbon storage is selected by fluctuating environments or simply tracks large metabolically versatile genomes.

directions.hypothesis: Per-segment contaminant and geochemical measurements will explain the east-west turnover and add explanatory power beyond hydrogeological zone, consistent with a plume entering from the northeast and moving southwest.
directions.outcomes: Support: geochemistry reduces the east-west signal and adds explanatory power beyond zone. Refute: zone explains the same variance with geochemistry added, or the east-west signal is unchanged. The catalog did not show the SSO tables, so their form is unconfirmed.
directions.prior_work: The Oak Ridge denitrifier papers (20305024, 22140175) and the soil biogeography paper (16407148) do not test hillslope versus east-west turnover or a plume gradient.
directions.question: Do measured geochemical gradients explain why SSO sediment communities differ by hydrogeological zone and turn over along the east-west axis rather than the hillslope?
directions.readiness_basis: The geochemistry is registered in CORAL but not loaded into the KBase Data Lakehouse, so this is a data-access step, and the catalog did not show the SSO community tables.
directions.test: Take the 221 SSO geochemistry samples already registered in CORAL, which are not yet in the KBase Data Lakehouse, and match them to the 37 sediment core segment communities. Fit a zone-only community model, then add measured contaminant concentrations. Test whether east-west turnover remains once geochemistry is included. Also compare VZ and VSZ directly against SZ1 and SZ2, and add pump-test groundwater data from wells L8, M5 and U2.
directions.title: Does a northeast-to-southwest contaminant gradient explain zone and east-west structure in SSO sediment communities?
directions.why_it_matters: If the plume explains community structure, community composition could serve as a map of contaminant transport. If zone alone explains it, the plume model is not needed.

directions.hypothesis: Early colonizers, such as copiotrophs favored by labile carbon, hold their positions through priority effects. History will therefore keep outweighing the current carbon source, and the memory index will decay only slowly over further passages.
directions.outcomes: Support: history still explains more variance than current carbon after the switch, and copiotroph-seeded communities keep their profile. Refute: current carbon takes over, or memory vanishes. Fungal ITS memory was not detectable at the earlier replicate level, so extra replicates also show whether that was low power.
directions.prior_work: The consortium papers (29169786, 41045130) and the carbon-use paper (14614618) do not test history against current substrate.
directions.question: Why does earlier enrichment history explain more of the later bacterial community variance than the current carbon source, and does the memory fade with further passaging?
directions.readiness_basis: The test needs new enrichment rounds, switches and added replicates that are not in the findings.
directions.test: Extend the lignin enrichment with added replicates and a Round 3 passage, including a reciprocal switch of carbon sources between lignin-only and lignin plus labile carbon histories. Inoculate copiotroph-enriched communities into lignin-only medium. Compare history and current-carbon effects on bacterial 16S, and add more replicates for fungal ITS. Add a no-lignin passage control.
directions.title: Does early enrichment history persist in lignin-degrading communities because of priority effects?
directions.why_it_matters: If history persists, enrichment outcomes depend on inoculum past and not only on the substrate. That would change how lignin-degrading consortia are designed and compared.

directions.hypothesis: Sulfate-reduction carriage in deep-clay Bacillota_B isolates reflects a few genera such as Desulfosporosinus. Deep-clay habitat adds no gene content beyond what those genera already carry.
directions.outcomes: Support: carriage matches genus identity and no deep-clay accessory genes appear. Refute: deep-clay isolates differ from same-genus baseline isolates, or deep-clay-specific accessory genes appear. With only 5 deep genomes, only large effects are detectable.
directions.prior_work: The Opalinus Clay and bentonite papers (27739431, 31852805, 37642485) describe sulfate reducers but do not control for phylogeny in a genome comparison.
directions.question: Within Bacillota_B, does carriage of dissimilatory sulfate reduction mark particular genera, or does it mark deep-clay habitat?
directions.readiness_basis: The genomes, taxonomy and annotations appear in the catalog; the genus-level comparison has not been run.
directions.test: Split the Bacillota_B genomes into genera using the GTDB taxonomy in the pangenome tables. Compare dsrAB-aprAB-sat carriage between the 5 deep-clay isolates and soil-baseline isolates within each genus. Use eggNOG annotations to search for accessory genes unique to deep clay. Re-check the iron-reduction contrast with the corrected markers.
directions.title: Is deep-clay sulfate reduction a genus-level trait of Bacillota_B or an adaptation to deep clay?
directions.why_it_matters: It would separate lineage effects from habitat selection in subsurface genomics. It would also show whether the deep-clay sulfate-reduction pattern is more than a sampling effect.

directions.hypothesis: Uranium alone does not set the growth advantage of these genera. In a factorial test of uranium and pH, pH or co-occurring factors will explain growth differences more than uranium does.
directions.outcomes: Support: pH or the second metal shapes growth more than uranium, or the lab responses do not match the field direction. Refute: uranium alone reproduces the field direction for both genera.
directions.prior_work: 30523276 links Rhodanobacter to uranium in the same aquifer. Neither it nor the Caulobacter uranium studies (33471994, 17905881) separate uranium from correlated chemistry for these two genera.
directions.question: Are the lower Caulobacter and higher Herbaspirillum abundances at high-uranium Oak Ridge sites caused by uranium itself, or by correlated factors such as pH?
directions.readiness_basis: The field correlations exist, but the factorial growth tests are new measurements.
directions.test: Grow Oak Ridge Caulobacter and Herbaspirillum isolates in a factorial design of uranium concentration and pH, with and without a second metal. Compare their growth responses with the field direction: lower for Caulobacter and higher for Herbaspirillum at high-uranium sites. Desulfovibrio is left out because its rarity made its field test unreliable.
directions.title: Do Caulobacter loss and Herbaspirillum gain at uranium sites reflect uranium tolerance or co-varying chemistry?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether field uranium trends can guide which organisms to test for uranium tolerance. It would also show whether they reflect general contamination.

directions.hypothesis: Quantitative metabolomics will show lower abundance of labile compounds in heated mineral soil. This fits depleted substrate and the methanotrophy and glyoxylate RNA signals.
directions.outcomes: Support: abundance falls for labile compound classes in heated soil, beyond detection counts. Refute: abundances are equal and only detection counts differ, pointing to detection limits.
directions.prior_work: The warming papers (28983050, 36448874) report reduced carbon availability, and 34512564 reports RNA responses. None measures metabolite detection or abundance in heated mineral soil.
directions.question: Does the lower number of detected metabolites in heated mineral soil reflect depleted metabolite pools, or detection limits?
directions.readiness_basis: The source says quantitative metabolomics layers exist in the lakehouse; the original project excluded them.
directions.test: Use the quantitative metabolomics layer for Harvard Forest samples, with the omics file tables to find samples. Compare compound abundances between heated and control mineral soil, not only detection counts. Examine whether detected compound classes match the methanotrophy and glyoxylate-cycle signals. Treat the RNA signals as a small pre-specified set.
directions.title: Does fewer detectable metabolites in heated Harvard Forest mineral soil reflect real depletion?
directions.why_it_matters: It would link substrate depletion, the leading explanation for warming responses, to measured chemistry in this soil. It would also say whether the unusual RNA signals have a chemical basis.

directions.hypothesis: A two-member consortium chosen for strong direct antagonism suppresses P. aeruginosa as well as a three-member consortium chosen for full niche coverage, even though its predicted coverage is much lower.
directions.outcomes: Support: the k=2 mixture matches k=3 suppression and supernatant alone reproduces much of it. Refute: k=3 clearly outperforms k=2 and supernatant has little effect, pointing to nutrient competition.
directions.prior_work: 27881418 and 37010413 show antagonism of pathogens by commensals or environmental pseudomonads, but none compares antagonism with nutrient coverage across consortium sizes.
directions.question: In defined commensal consortia for cystic fibrosis airways, does direct killing or inhibition of the pathogen explain suppression better than overlap in nutrient use?
directions.readiness_basis: Requires new mixture assays and mouse work; the existing scores assume additive inhibition and cannot separate the mechanisms.
directions.test: Grow the k=2 and k=3 consortia from the formulation design (including M. luteus ASMA-2965, N. mucosa ASMA-3643, S. salivarius ASMA-737) against PA14 in defined media and in cell-free supernatant, separating contact-independent antagonism from nutrient competition. Include a strain typed ExoS+ alongside PA14. Measure mixtures directly rather than assuming additive inhibition, then compare in a mouse colonization model.
directions.title: Does direct antagonism, rather than niche coverage, drive commensal suppression of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
directions.why_it_matters: The design disagreement over two versus three organisms decides which consortia go forward to animal testing. If antagonism dominates, engraftable two-member designs are justified. If coverage dominates, persistence of poorly engrafting species becomes the key problem.

directions.hypothesis: At least one substrate class predicted by genomic pathway analysis but not yet tested, such as a sugar alcohol or polyamine, supports growth of candidate commensals at a clearly higher rate than P. aeruginosa.
directions.outcomes: Support: a substrate where commensals grow and P. aeruginosa grows poorly. Refute: all predicted substrates are used equally well by the pathogen, extending the null result.
directions.prior_work: 17873029 describes sputum nutrition and P. aeruginosa substrate preferences, but no retrieved paper screens substrates for selectivity toward commensals.
directions.question: Do substrates missing from the 22 tested carbon sources give selective growth to protective commensals over P. aeruginosa?
directions.readiness_basis: Pathway predictions are in the catalog; the growth assays are new measurements.
directions.test: Score pathway completeness for sugar-alcohol, polyamine and mucin-derived sugar catabolism across genomes of P. aeruginosa and the candidate commensals using the pangenome pathway predictions. Then run sole-carbon growth assays for the top predicted substrates on the candidate commensals and on P. aeruginosa strains of both ExoU+ and ExoS+ types.
directions.title: Can untested nutrients such as mucins, polyamines or sugar alcohols favor commensals over Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
directions.why_it_matters: No selective prebiotic was found among the tested substrates. A selective one would let a formulation be paired with a feeding strategy that does not depend on engraftment alone.

directions.hypothesis: Within species that contain both carriers and non-carriers, genomes with a SNIPE-type gene differ in environmental embedding from non-carriers, rather than the species-level difference arising only from which species carry it.
directions.outcomes: Support: within-species carrier and non-carrier genomes differ in environment in many species. Refute: differences vanish within species, so the niche signal reflects which species carry SNIPE.
directions.prior_work: 42725772 links retron distribution to ecological niche and 41741653 gives the SNIPE mechanism, but neither tests within-species habitat differences for SNIPE.
directions.question: SNIPE-bearing species occupy distinct environments, and most SNIPE genes are accessory. Within a species, do carrier genomes come from different habitats than non-carriers?
directions.readiness_basis: The tables are in the catalog, but the carrier labelling and stratified comparison have to be computed; some hits may be non-SNIPE proteins.
directions.test: Identify DUF4041-containing gene clusters in pangenome species, label genomes as carriers or non-carriers, and join to environmental embeddings and isolation metadata. Compare carrier and non-carrier genomes within each species, using species as a stratum. Note that embedding coverage is limited and biased toward environmental isolates.
directions.title: Does SNIPE carriage within a species track habitat, beyond species-level niche differences?
directions.why_it_matters: It separates a taxonomic explanation of SNIPE distribution from a habitat-linked one. This is the first step before asking whether habitat-specific phage exposure matters; this analysis does not measure phage pressure.

directions.hypothesis: SNIPE-like proteins outside Enterobacterales pair DUF4041 with a limited set of alternative nuclease domains, such as Mug113, in a lineage-specific pattern.
directions.outcomes: Support: recurrent non-GIY-YIG nuclease partners with clear lineage structure. Refute: DUF4041 pairs mainly with unrelated domains, so most hits are not defence proteins.
directions.prior_work: 41741653 characterizes SNIPE in E. coli against phage lambda but does not survey nuclease partners or archaeal homologues.
directions.question: Since no gene cluster paired DUF4041 with canonical GIY-YIG, and the archaeal homologue carries a Mug113 nuclease domain, which nuclease partners do SNIPE-like proteins use across lineages?
directions.readiness_basis: Annotation tables are in the catalog; divergent homologues may be missed by the annotations, and the experiments are new.
directions.test: Tabulate Pfam co-occurrence for DUF4041-containing clusters across phyla using the pangenome annotations, flagging nuclease-bearing architectures. Compare with the Methanococcus maripaludis homologue (MMJJ_RS01635), whose mutant fitness was mild under formate/acetate and near neutral elsewhere. Then test candidate nuclease architectures for phage-DNA cleavage in a heterologous host.
directions.title: Do SNIPE-like proteins pair DUF4041 with nuclease domains other than GIY-YIG?
directions.why_it_matters: It would show whether the E. coli SNIPE mechanism is one member of a wider family, and whether broad homologue counts include proteins that are not defence nucleases.
